text:
So you ran an experiment, or maybe something that looks like an experiment, and you got a result. Great. But how do you know the result is real? That is what causal robustness is all about. It is a collection of frameworks, each one designed to attack your causal claim from a different angle. If your claim survives multiple attacks, you can start to trust it. If it falls apart under the first test, well, better to find out now.

We are going to walk through ten frameworks, and we will use the same example throughout so everything stays concrete. The example is this. You have a synthetic population, think of it like a simulated society. Some agents in this population are exposed to a political ad. Others are not. You observe that the exposed group shifts their voting intention by about eight percentage points. The question is, did the ad actually cause that shift, or is something else going on?

Let us start with the first framework, E-values. An E-value answers a very specific question. How strong would an unmeasured confounder need to be to completely explain away your observed effect? It gives you a single number. In our example, the eight percentage point shift corresponds to a risk ratio of about 1.5, and the E-value comes out to 2.4. What that means is, some hidden variable would need to be associated with both ad exposure and voting intention by a factor of at least 2.4 each to wipe out the effect. If the strongest confounder you know about, say party affiliation, only has a factor of 1.8, then your estimate looks pretty sturdy. But here is the catch. The E-value cannot tell you whether such a confounder actually exists. A high E-value means your result is hard to explain away. It does not mean it is definitely causal.

The second framework is Rosenbaum Sensitivity Bounds. This is the go to tool when you have done propensity score matching. You matched exposed and unexposed agents on demographics, media diet, prior political leaning, and so on. But there might be hidden bias, some factor you did not match on. Rosenbaum bounds ask, how much hidden bias would it take to change your conclusion? You crank up a parameter called Gamma from one upward and watch what happens to your p-value. In our example, at Gamma equals 1.8 the p-value crosses 0.05. So a hidden factor that made agents 1.8 times more likely to see the ad, and independently shifted their vote, would kill the result. Is that plausible? That is a judgment call you have to make based on what you know about your synthetic world.
